A toboggan is a type of sled — a flat, narrow vehicle designed for sliding down snow-covered slopes for fun or sport.
What makes a toboggan different from other sleds?

Most sleds you might imagine have metal blades (called runners) on the bottom, like two thin rails. A toboggan is different: it has no runners at all. Its bottom is completely flat and smooth — it sits directly on the snow. This flat surface lets it glide across the snow rather than cut into it, which means it can travel very smoothly and pick up quite a bit of speed.

The other defining feature is its front end, which curves upward — much like the tip of a ski or the front of a boat. This upward curve is not decorative; it serves a purpose. Without it, the front edge would dig into the snow as the sled moves forward and bring it to a sudden stop. The curve allows the sled to ride over the snow gracefully instead.

Traditionally, a toboggan is long and narrow, made from thin strips of wood (such as birch or maple) bent and tied together. The wooden strips run lengthwise from the curved front all the way to the flat back. Because of this long design, a toboggan can comfortably carry more than one person — riders sit in a single-file line, one behind the other, with their legs stretched forward. The person in front faces the slope; everyone else follows behind them.

Modern toboggans are often made of plastic rather than wood, but the essential shape remains the same: flat bottom, curved front, long enough for a group.

You take a toboggan to the top of a snowy hill, place it on the ground with the curved end pointing downhill, sit on it, and push off. The sled then slides down the slope, carrying its riders at high speed. Because there are no runners to steer with, controlling a toboggan is quite limited — riders steer by shifting their body weight or by dragging a foot in the snow. This lack of control is part of what makes tobogganing feel wild and exciting.

It is primarily a recreational winter activity, very popular in Canada, the northern United States, and parts of Europe. Children and adults alike use toboggans for winter fun on snowy hillsides.

In certain parts of the southern United States (particularly in Appalachian and southeastern regions), the word toboggan is also used informally to refer to a knitted winter hat — the kind that covers your ears and fits snugly over your head (elsewhere called a beanie, ski cap, or woolly hat). This usage is strictly regional; most English speakers outside that area would not recognize it. If you hear an American from the South say "I forgot my toboggan," they almost certainly mean their warm hat, not a sled.
Think of a toboggan as a long, flat wooden tray with a curled-up nose — built for a group of people to pile onto and shoot down a snowy hill together. That image captures its essence completely.
